Currently
column2: we try to ensure that we use vcnum of 0 on the first

column1: established session on a connection and then try to use a different
vcnum on each session after that.
This is a little odd
column2: since there's no real reason to use a different

column1: vcnum for each SMB session. I can only assume there was some confusion
between SMB sessions and VCs. That's somewhat understandable since they
both get created during SESSION_SETUP
that they are really orthogonal. The comment on max_vcs in particular
looks quite misguided. An SMB session is already uniquely identified
by the SMB UID value -- there's no need to again uniquely ID with a
VC.
Furthermore
column2: a vcnum of 0 is a cue to the server that it should release

column1: any resources that were previously held by the client. This sounds like
a good thing
a) it totally ignores the fact that other programs on the box (e.g.
smbclient) might have connections established to the server. Using a
vcnum of 0 causes them to get kicked off.
b) it causes problems with NAT. If several clients are connected to the
same server via the same NAT'ed address
server it kicks off all the others
column2: which then reconnect and kick off

column1: the first one...ad nauseum.
I don't see any reason to ignore the advice in ""Implementing CIFS"" which
has a comprehensive treatment of virtual circuits. In there
...and contrary to the specs the client should always use a VcNumber of
one
Have the client just use a hardcoded vcnum of 1
special behavior of vcnum 0.
